Fit a random forest with ranger

Source: R/model-rf.R
fit_rf_model.Rd

Fits a regression random forest on an sf layer and returns it as a spatial_fit, so it works with cv_spatial(), predict_surface(), area_of_applicability() and the plot() method like any other backend. A forest suits a response that is non-linear in its predictors when predictive accuracy matters more than an interpretable model.

Usage

fit_rf_model(
  data_sf,
  response_var,
  predictor_vars,
  num_trees = 500L,
  mtry = NULL,
  min_node_size = NULL,
  importance = c("permutation", "impurity", "none"),
  include_coords = FALSE,
  replace = TRUE,
  sample_fraction = NULL,
  seed = 123L,
  num_threads = NULL,
  .already_prepped = FALSE,
  ...
)

Arguments

data_sf

An sf object with response, predictors and geometry.

response_var

Response column name.

predictor_vars

Predictor column names.

num_trees

Number of trees. Default 500.

mtry

Predictors sampled per split. NULL uses ranger's default.

min_node_size

Minimum node size. NULL uses ranger's default.

importance

"permutation" (default), "impurity" or "none". Impurity importance is biased towards continuous and high-cardinality predictors (Strobl et al. 2007), so permutation importance is the default although it costs more.

include_coords

Add the coordinates as predictors. Default FALSE, which leaves the forest with no spatial information; see Coordinates as predictors.

replace

Logical; grow each tree on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement (TRUE, ranger's default and this one) or on a subsample drawn without replacement (FALSE). Strobl et al. (2007) show that bootstrap sampling with replacement is itself a source of bias in variable importance toward predictors with many distinct values or categories, and recommend subsampling without replacement. The forest's predictions change slightly with the choice. The setting is recorded in $info and printed with the fit.

sample_fraction

Fraction of rows drawn for each tree. NULL (default) uses ranger's rule: all rows when replace = TRUE, 0.632 (the expected share of distinct rows in a bootstrap sample) when replace = FALSE. A single number in (0, 1] overrides it. replace = FALSE with sample_fraction = 1 grows every tree on every row, so nothing is out of bag: the fit warns (see "Fitted values are out-of-bag").

seed

Seed passed to ranger. Default 123.

num_threads

Threads for ranger. Default NULL means getOption("mc.cores", 1L): one thread unless the session has set more, the convention brms and parallel use. Predictions do not depend on the thread count; pass parallel::detectCores() to use every core.

.already_prepped

Internal; leave at the default.

...

Passed to ranger::ranger(). ranger's own spellings of the arguments this function already sets (num.trees, min.node.size, num.threads, mtry, importance, seed, replace, sample.fraction, x, y) are rejected with a message naming the wrapper argument to use instead. respect.unordered.factors passed here overrides the "order" this function sets when a predictor is categorical; see Categorical predictors.

Value

An rf_fit object (inherits from spatial_fit). $info carries num_trees, mtry, min_node_size, importance_type, importance (a named numeric, or NULL when importance = "none"), include_coords, categorical_predictors (the unordered factor and character predictors, possibly none) and respect_unordered_factors (how ranger was told to split them: "order" unless overridden through ..., and NA when there is none and nothing was passed), replace and sample_fraction (the sampling each tree was grown on, with sample_fraction resolved to the number ranger used), oob_rmse and oob_r_squared (each NA_real_ when ranger did not compute it; forwarding oob.error = FALSE through ... is one way to get there), fitted_are_oob (always TRUE; summary() reads it to label its metrics), seed and n_dropped (the rows prep_model_data() removed for missing or non-finite values or a bad geometry, so $n can be read against nrow(data_sf)), and response_centre and response_scale (below). The raw forest is in $engine.

The forest is grown on the response taken about its centre where that centre is more than 1000 times the response's spread (as at 1e8 plus a spread of 1), and divided by a power of two where the response is so large or its spread so small that its squares overflow or lose their bits (beyond about 1e100 or 1e-100). The splits of a forest do not change under a shift or a scale of the response, and ranger's split scores, formed from squares of the response, read the rounding of the offset otherwise. $info$response_centre (0 where none is taken) and $info$response_scale (1 where none is applied) record them, and they are put back on fitted(), predict(), residuals(), oob_rmse and importance (squared units, so multiplied by the scale twice; beyond the range of doubles it is Inf or loses its bits, and a WARN line says so). The permutation importance under scale.permutation.importance = TRUE and the impurity importance under splitrule = "maxstat" have no units and are left as ranger reports them. The forest in $engine predicts (y - response_centre) / response_scale, and its own predictions and prediction.error are in those units. Every other response is passed to ranger as it is.

Coordinates as predictors

include_coords = TRUE adds the x and y coordinates to the predictors. They are the only spatial information a forest can be given: without them it sees the covariates alone, and print() says "no spatial information used". The default is FALSE.

The gain from the coordinates depends on where the predictions are wanted. A forest splits on location as on any column, so it follows the training surface closely between sampled points, and has only the nearest edge of the data to go on beyond them. Between sampled points the coordinates can lower the error, most where the covariates carry little of the spatial structure themselves, and the gain fades with distance from the training data. Beyond the autocorrelation range, or in an area the data never visited, the coordinates can make predictions worse (Meyer et al. 2019). With covariates that carry the spatial structure themselves, expect less from the coordinates.

Score the forests with and without coordinates on the same folds, at the distances the map will be used at (see "Fold methods" in make_folds(); "Out-of-bag error" below says why the out-of-bag error does not serve). Build the folds once and pass them to cv_rf() with and without the coordinates:


folds   <- make_folds(dat, k = 5, method = "block_kfold")
plain   <- cv_rf(dat, "z", c("a", "b"), folds = folds)
with_xy <- cv_rf(dat, "z", c("a", "b"), folds = folds,
                 include_coords = TRUE)
c(plain = plain$overall$RMSE, with_xy = with_xy$overall$RMSE)

The example on cv_rf() runs this comparison and reads it fold by fold. Setting include_coords = TRUE logs this advice once per session, as a log line rather than an R warning, and not once for every fold of a cross-validation.

Categorical predictors

A predictor that is an unordered factor or a character column is split with respect.unordered.factors = "order": ranger orders its levels by mean response once, before growing, and splits on that order, the handling ranger's own help recommends. ranger's default for a regression forest, "ignore", splits on the order the levels are stored in (alphabetical, for most data), which for a nominal variable is arbitrary. Pass respect.unordered.factors through ... to choose otherwise ("ignore", or "partition" for every two-way split of the levels, which is slow beyond a few levels). Ordered factors are left alone and split on their own order, and with splitrule = "extratrees" ranger's own default for that rule, "partition", is kept. The setting is recorded in $info$respect_unordered_factors and printed with the fit.

Out-of-bag error

ranger's out-of-bag (OOB) error holds each observation out of the trees that did not sample it. That is a random hold-out: the trees that did not see a point almost always saw its neighbours, so under spatial autocorrelation it is the error of predicting among the samples, as random k-fold is, and reads low for predictions made farther from the data than the samples sit from each other (see make_folds()). It is reported as $info$oob_rmse and $info$oob_r_squared and labelled as OOB wherever it appears. Use cv_rf() for a spatial estimate.

Fitted values are out-of-bag

fitted() on an rf_fit returns out-of-bag predictions, as the random forest packages themselves do. In-sample predictions from a forest come close to reproducing the training data, and their \(R^2\) says little about new data. summary() therefore reports out-of-bag metrics for a forest and in-sample metrics for a GWR or a Bayesian GP fit, and the two do not compare; compare_models_cv() scores every backend on the same folds.

A row that every tree sampled has no out-of-bag prediction, and ranger reports NaN for it. That is every row under replace = FALSE with sample_fraction = 1, and a few under a small num_trees. The fit warns with the count; fitted() and residuals() are NaN on those rows, and summary() says how many rows its metrics were computed on. With no row out of bag at all, the OOB error (NA in $info$oob_rmse and $info$oob_r_squared) and the permutation importance (NaN) are undefined too, and print() says so. cv_rf() scores its fold forests on the held-out rows, never out of bag, so it warns once with the number of folds affected rather than once per fold.

References

Meyer, H., Reudenbach, C., Wöllauer, S. and Nauss, T. (2019). Importance of spatial predictor variable selection in machine learning applications – moving from data reproduction to spatial prediction. Ecological Modelling 411, 108815. doi:10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2019.108815

Strobl, C., Boulesteix, A.-L., Zeileis, A. and Hothorn, T. (2007). Bias in random forest variable importance measures: illustrations, sources and a solution. BMC Bioinformatics 8, 25. doi:10.1186/1471-2105-8-25

See also

cv_rf() to score the forest on spatial folds; predict() (spatial_fit-predict) and predict_surface() to predict; area_of_applicability() to mark where the predictions apply (it weights the predictors by this forest's importance).

Other model fitting: fit_bayesian_spatial_model(), fit_gwr_model(), gp_lengthscale_bounds(), new_spatial_fit()

Examples

library(sf)
set.seed(1)
n <- 150
dat <- st_as_sf(
  data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000),
             a = rnorm(n), b = rnorm(n)),
  coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632
)
dat$z <- 2 * dat$a - dat$b + rnorm(n, 0, 0.3)
fit <- fit_rf_model(dat, "z", c("a", "b"))
fit
#> <Random Forest (ranger)> spatial model fit
#>   Formula : z ~ a + b
#>   n       : 150
#>   CRS     : EPSG:32632
#>   Trees   : 500 (mtry = 1, min node = 5)
#>   Coords as predictors: no - no spatial information used; see ?fit_rf_model
#>   Sampling: bootstrap, with replacement (100.0% of rows per tree)
#>   OOB RMSE: 0.6995   OOB R^2: 0.9093
#>   Importance (permutation): a=6.886, b=1.583
#> 
#>   OOB is a random hold-out: under spatial autocorrelation it is the error
#>   of predicting among the samples, and reads low for predictions made
#>   farther from the data than the samples sit from each other. Score a map
#>   that predicts farther with cv_rf() on folds at its distances
#>   (?fold_separation).
fit$info$importance     # permutation importance of a and b
#>        a        b 
#> 6.886377 1.583079
